`using x = getResource()` calls `x[Symbol.dispose]()` automatically when the block exits, even on a throw, and multiple `using` declarations dispose in reverse order; `await using` does the same with `Symbol.asyncDispose`. TypeScript compiles the syntax, but the runtime still needs `Symbol.dispose` to exist (a polyfill on older Node), and the tsconfig lib needs the esnext disposable types. `as const` changes the inferred type: literals stay literal and everything becomes readonly, but it checks nothing. `satisfies` checks the value against a type without changing the inferred type, so typos and missing keys error while you keep the precise type. You can combine them: `as const satisfies Config`. Action: none.

Use `useLayoutEffect` when you need to read or change the DOM before the browser paints, such as measuring an element and positioning a tooltip, so the user never sees a flash of the wrong layout. `useEffect` runs after paint and is the right default for everything else (data fetching, subscriptions). They're different. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive just reuses a TCP connection for the next request, but requests still go one at a time per connection, so browsers open several connections to parallelise. HTTP/2 multiplexes many concurrent request/response streams over one connection with framing and header compression. TCP-level head-of-line blocking still exists on h2, which is what HTTP/3 addresses. Action: none.

A Deployment treats pods as interchangeable: random names, any pod can be replaced or scaled freely, storage is typically shared or absent. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable identity (ordered names like db-0, db-1), stable network names and its own persistent volume, and rolls out in order. Pick it for databases, queues and clustered systems where a replica must keep its identity and data. Action: none.
